claims.text: The conventional baseline is a boride coating without chromium doping.
Chromium can be incorporated at a minor, controlled concentration into the boride coating through the coating-processing route.
Chromium addition will produce a chromium-enriched oxide layer on the coating surface.
The chromium-enriched oxide will also form along grain boundaries of the boride coating.
Chromium in the coating will preferentially oxidize during molten-aluminum service.
Preferential chromium oxidation will form a stable, continuous chromium-rich oxide.
The continuous chromium-rich oxide will act as a barrier limiting direct interaction between molten aluminum and the underlying boride.
Limiting molten-aluminum contact with the boride will reduce coating degradation and mass loss.
A chromium-doped boride coating will exhibit lower mass loss than an otherwise comparable chromium-free boride coating under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
The proposed protection requires an oxygen potential that permits chromium oxidation.
Significant changes in temperature, atmospheric oxygen content, or immersion duration may alter the coating's protective performance.
Prior literature on similar alloying strategies suggests that chromium addition could meaningfully reduce corrosion.
